lead: A haptic display creates controlled force, vibration or skin deformation on the user. It exists because seeing and hearing a virtual object is not enough when the task needs contact: pressing a virtual button, feeling a tool touch tissue, or holding a virtual cricket bat. Haptic displays are used in surgical simulators, teleoperation, assembly planning, game controllers and phone keyboards. This chapter groups them by what they push: the whole limb (force feedback) or only the skin (tactile feedback).
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for the three output channels.

blocks.text: Force feedback, also called kinesthetic feedback, pushes the arm or hand. It controls force at the handle in newtons (N) or torque at a joint in newton-metres (N·m). A grounded arm is fixed to a table and ends in a pen or handle. Motors at the joints resist your hand. The Phantom family is a common pen-style example. Its workspace is a box of tens of centimetres, its maximum handle force is about 3 N to 4 N, and it updates at about 1 kHz.

An exoskeleton is worn on the arm or hand. It controls joint torque, often 0.1 N·m to 1 N·m, and finger force of a few N; its workspace follows the human joint range. A cable-driven system has motors on a frame and cables to the handle. It can cover metres and pull tens to hundreds of N, with update rates from 100 Hz to 500 Hz. A motion platform moves the whole body. It controls displacement in metres and updates at tens of hertz. All force devices have a saturation force: the maximum they can push. They also have a finite workspace.

sections.h3: Tactile feedback acts on the skin

blocks.text: Tactile feedback acts on the skin. Vibrotactile actuators are the most common. An eccentric rotating mass (ERM) motor spins an off-centre mass; a linear resonant actuator (LRA) drives a mass along one axis at resonance; a piezoelectric actuator bends a plate. They control vibration frequency in hertz (Hz) and amplitude in micrometres (µm). ERM and LRA units often run at 100 Hz to 300 Hz with amplitudes of a few µm to hundreds of µm, and update at about 1 kHz.

A pin array moves small pins up and down by about 0.5 mm to 1 mm, with millinewtons (mN) per pin; update is around 100 Hz. A thermal display uses Peltier cells to heat or cool the skin by a few °C, but it is slow, about 1 Hz to 10 Hz. An air-jet display blows a small nozzle of air at the skin; its spatial resolution is a few millimetres and update is tens of hertz. An electrotactile display passes small currents through electrodes to excite nerves; it has no moving parts and controls current in milliamperes and pulse width in microseconds.

Surface haptics adds a tactile effect to a touchscreen. It may vibrate the glass or control friction under the finger with a lateral force of a few mN. Phones use it for key clicks; car dashboards use it to confirm a touch without looking.

The hand is a fine sensor, but a haptic device has a small workspace compared with graphics. A desktop arm may move your hand 20 cm; a head-mounted display fills your whole field of view. The visual channel can update at 60 Hz to 120 Hz. A haptic loop often needs about 1 kHz, because a stiff virtual wall becomes unstable at low loop rates (see Chapter 3.8). Human sensing limits are in Chapter 3.7.

figure.caption: The straight line is the force the virtual wall asks for, F = 1500 N/m × x; the flat part is the most the motors can give. At 2 mm penetration the pen pushes 3.0 N, and past 2.2 mm the force stays at 3.3 N, so the wall feels soft.

spec.aria: A graph of handle force against wall penetration for a pen-style force-feedback arm with stiffness 1500 N per metre: the wall demand rises as a straight line to 4.5 N at 3 mm, while the device output rises with it and then flattens at the 3.3 N saturation limit from 2.2 mm onwards, passing through 3.0 N at 2 mm.

examples.question: A pen-style force-feedback arm renders a rigid wall with a virtual spring of stiffness k = 1500 N/m. The motors saturate at 3.3 N. Find the force at 2 mm penetration and the deepest penetration that can still be rendered.
steps: Write the data with consistent units: k = 1500 N/m, Fmax = 3.3 N, x = 2 mm = 0.002 m.
Use the spring law F = kx. F = 1500 × 0.002 = 3.0 N.
Compare with saturation: 3.0 N is less than 3.3 N, so the device can render this force.
At saturation, Fmax = k x_sat. So x_sat = Fmax / k = 3.3 / 1500 = 0.0022 m.
Beyond 2.2 mm the device cannot push harder, so the wall feels soft.
examples.answer: The force at 2 mm penetration is 3.0 N, and the deepest renderable penetration is 0.0022 m, or 2.2 mm.
examples.check:
k = 1500.0
Fmax = 3.3
x = 0.002
F = k * x
x_sat = Fmax / k
print(F)
print(x_sat)
print(x_sat * 1000)

traps: Treating tactile feedback and force feedback as the same thing. Force feedback pushes the whole limb; tactile feedback moves only the skin.
Forgetting that the device has a saturation force and a finite workspace. A virtual wall becomes soft once the motors saturate.
Quoting motor torque when the question asks for force at the handle. Torque is in N·m; handle force is in N.
Mixing millimetres and metres in F = kx. A 2 mm penetration is 0.002 m, not 2 m.
Confusing update rate with vibration frequency. Update rate is how often the loop runs in Hz; vibration frequency is the buzz you feel in Hz.

quiz.a: A haptic display is a device that creates controlled force, vibration or skin deformation on the user to simulate touch or contact.

quiz.q: What is another name for force feedback?
Why does a haptic loop often need about 1 kHz while graphics can run at 60 Hz?
quiz.a: A haptic device is in contact with a virtual spring. Low loop rate adds delay and makes a stiff wall unstable. The eye tolerates 60 Hz for motion, so graphics can update more slowly.

quiz.q: A grounded arm has stiffness k = 2000 N/m and saturates at 4 N. Find the force at 1.5 mm penetration and the saturation penetration.
A wall has k = 1500 N/m and the device saturates at 3.3 N. At 3 mm penetration, what force does the wall ask for and what force does the user feel?
quiz.a: The wall asks for F = 1500 × 0.003 = 4.5 N. The device can give only 3.3 N. The user feels 3.3 N, so the wall feels softer than intended.

quiz.q: State one difference between an ERM motor and an LRA.
quiz.a: An ERM spins an off-centre mass, so frequency depends on speed. An LRA drives a mass along one axis at resonance, giving a faster response and a narrower frequency band.

quiz.q: Why can a pin array not render a rigid wall?
quiz.a: A pin array moves only the skin by about 1 mm and uses millinewton forces per pin. It cannot stop the whole hand or supply the newtons needed to resist a stiff wall. A rigid wall needs force feedback.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research moves toward mid-air ultrasound haptics, wearable arrays and texture rendering on touchscreens. Industry uses haptics in surgical robots, automotive touchscreens and consumer VR controllers. Search for 'surface haptics', 'ultrasound haptic feedback' and 'haptic rendering stability' to go further.
